title: A reflex is not the pain

scenes.tts: A mouse has a nerve injury, and a touch makes its paw pull away. Is that the pain? A withdrawal reflex is cheap to measure. It is also easy to mistake for pain. An unpleasant experience is a different measurement. Most pain assays record the first. So where does the second one live?
scenes.visual: Stimulus chip, arrow, reflex meter rises; a dashed question box for the unpleasant experience; a label marks the reflex as what most assays record.
scenes.narration: A mouse has a nerve injury, and a touch makes its paw pull away. Is that the pain? A withdrawal reflex is cheap to measure. It is also easy to mistake for pain. An unpleasant experience is a different measurement. Most pain assays record the first. So where does the second one live?

scenes.tts: Corder and colleagues asked a sharp question. Does a defined set of neurons carry the second measurement? They worked in male mice with a nerve injury. Two endpoints can be measured. One is the withdrawal reflex. The other is affective-motivational behaviour, such as escape and avoidance.
scenes.visual: Two meters side by side, reflex and escape-avoidance; a cluster box with a question mark appears beside them; scope chips for male mice and nerve injury.
scenes.narration: Corder and colleagues asked a sharp question. Does a defined set of neurons carry the second measurement? They worked in male mice with a nerve injury. Two endpoints can be measured. One is the withdrawal reflex. The other is affective-motivational behaviour, such as escape and avoidance.

scenes.tts: First, in male mice, they imaged principal neurons in the basolateral amygdala. They imaged the same mice in repeated sessions. They identified an ensemble, a set of cells that respond together. It responded to noxious stimuli. And it encoded their negative valence. Valence means how bad or good a stimulus is.
scenes.visual: Large cluster of grey cells in a basolateral amygdala box; a noxious stimulus chip arrives and a subset lights up as the ensemble; a negative valence chip appears.
scenes.narration: First, in male mice, they imaged principal neurons in the basolateral amygdala. They imaged the same mice in repeated sessions. They identified an ensemble, a set of cells that respond together. It responded to noxious stimuli. And it encoded their negative valence. Valence means how bad or good a stimulus is.

scenes.tts: Then came the nerve injury in these mice. After the injury, innocuous stimuli also recruited that ensemble. An innocuous stimulus is one that is normally not painful. So the cells that encoded negative valence were now recruited by innocuous stimuli.
scenes.visual: Cells reset to grey; label changes to after nerve injury; an innocuous stimulus chip arrives and the same cells light.
scenes.narration: Then came the nerve injury in these mice. After the injury, innocuous stimuli also recruited that ensemble. An innocuous stimulus is one that is normally not painful. So the cells that encoded negative valence were now recruited by innocuous stimuli.

scenes.tts: This tested whether the two endpoints could be pulled apart. Next, they tagged the active neurons genetically. This used activity-dependent tagging. Then they silenced the tagged ensemble in nerve-injured male mice. The affective-motivational pain behaviours fell. The measured withdrawal reflexes were preserved. The paw still pulled away, but the escape and avoidance fell away. The two endpoints came apart.
scenes.visual: Cluster slides left, both meters appear high; ensemble cells get a tag ring then go silenced; the escape meter falls, the reflex meter holds.
scenes.narration: This tested whether the two endpoints could be pulled apart. Next, they tagged the active neurons genetically. This used activity-dependent tagging. Then they silenced the tagged ensemble in nerve-injured male mice. The affective-motivational pain behaviours fell. The measured withdrawal reflexes were preserved. The paw still pulled away, but the escape and avoidance fell away. The two endpoints came apart.

scenes.tts: Now read the scope. This is male mice, a nerve injury model, and the behaviours the authors chose. A mouse gives no verbal report. So the result separates two measurable endpoints, in one species and one assay. It does not show that unpleasantness is made in the basolateral amygdala. It does not show that silencing it abolishes sensing of the stimulus. It says nothing about other regions. Keep this rule. A withdrawal reflex is not a measure of how unpleasant a stimulus is.
scenes.visual: Scope chips; a shows column with two separated endpoints and a does-not-show column with two struck-out claims; final rule line.
